Response to correspondence by Dr Aamar on ‘EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs: 2025 update’
Sequential disease activity assessment for predicting future treatment trajectories in patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with JAK inhibitors: a group-based trajectory and landmark analysis
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to identify disease activity trajectories in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treated with Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors and to determine whether early disease activity improved prediction of long-term treatment trajectories. Methods We analysed 843 patients treated with JAK inhibitors from a multicentre registry. Group-based trajectory modelling was used to identify distinct Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) trajectories over 52 weeks. Landmark analyses at weeks 4 and 12 were performed using multivariate logistic regression with multiple imputations. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, Brier score, and bootstrap-based internal validation. Results Four distinct trajectory groups were identified: rapid responders (64.9%), partial responders with persistent residual disease activity (18.1%), responders with high baseline disease activity (12.7%), and persistent nonresponders (4.3%). Week-52 remission rates ranged from 0.0% to 47.7% across the groups. Incorporating the CDAI at landmark time points substantially improved the prediction of a favourable trajectory, whereas the CDAI slope provided minimal additional predictive value. Brier scores improved markedly after incorporating week-12 CDAI, with minimal further improvement after CDAI slope inclusion. Bootstrap validation demonstrated minimal optimism and good calibration. The optimal CDAI thresholds for predicting a favourable trajectory were 12.0 and 9.3 at weeks 4 and 12, respectively. Conclusions Early disease activity dynamically refined the prediction of future treatment trajectories in patients with RA treated with JAK inhibitors. The absolute CDAI at landmark time points was more informative than change-based metrics, supporting sequential disease activity assessment for time-anchored treatment decision-making.

title: A new humanised TCR transgenic mouse model to study T cells reactive to citrullinated tenascin C, a relevant autoantigen in rheumatoid arthritis
abstract: Abstract Objectives Autoreactive T cells recognizing citrullinated antigens, although rare and difficult to study, are implicated in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). To allow functional studies and manipulation of such T cells, we have generated and characterized transgenic mice expressing a TCR cloned from an RA patient and reactive with a prominent target, citrullinated tenascin C (citTNC). Methods A humanized TCR transgenic (hTCR-tg) mouse recognizing the citrullinated TNC22 (citTNC22) antigen in an HLA-DRB1*04:01 (HLA-DR4) restricted manner was developed by genetically engineering a chimeric TCR expressing murine constant domains and human V(D)J sequences. hTCR-tg mice were immune phenotyped in murine H-2 b and humanized HLA-DR4 backgrounds using full spectrum flow cytometry, cytokine ELISAs and fluorospot assays at steady-state and after antigen challenge. Additionally, we investigated the presence of antibodies to citTNC and arthritis following citTNC protein immunization. Results Thymic selection of hTCR T cells differed between the two MHC-II alleles, with a normal CD4+ T cell development observed solely under HLA-DR4 restriction. The chimeric hTCR maintained its citTNC22 specificity in vitro and ex vivo, without cross-reactivity to native TNC22 or other citrullinated autoantigens. hTCR-tg CD4+ T cells responded to antigen challenge in vivo and provided support to IgG class-switch and antigen-specific antibody production. Moreover, protein immunized hTCR-tg mice developed arthritis after periarticular challenge with citTNC. Conclusions hTCR-tg mice expressing an RA patient-derived autoreactive TCR develop functional antigen-specific and HLA-restricted CD4+ T cells. The combination of humanized HLA-DR4 and TNC22 mice will be a valuable tool in the development of antigen-specific therapies translatable to human disease.

title: Conceptual framework for the definition of disease modification in systemic sclerosis and potential implications for drug development and clinical study design
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multifaceted systemic autoimmune disease, characterised by the interplay of vascular alterations, immune dysregulation, and fibrosis. The molecular changes and the clinical presentation of SSc are highly heterogeneous and vary considerably between individual patients. This heterogeneity has hampered efforts to reach a unified and pragmatic definition of disease modification in SSc. Using a consensus approach among SSc experts, the authors seek to identify current challenges in defining SSc disease modification. The definition of disease modification in SSc requires a nuanced approach that considers molecular, mechanistic, and clinical aspects. Disease-modifying treatments in SSc should target core pathways or cells rather than regulatory mechanisms. Disease-modifying treatments should show sustained effects on disease activity and prevent progression of damage across organs, manifestations, disease stages, and disease endotypes. The complex and variable nature of SSc needs to be reflected in preclinical drug development efforts and clinical trial designs to demonstrate disease-modifying effects of drug candidates for SSc. We herein provide a first framework for the definition of disease modification of vascular, inflammatory, and fibrotic domains in SSc. Advances in our understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving the progression of SSc will enable further refinement of the definition of disease modification and guide optimal preclinical modelling and innovative clinical trial design in future efforts.

title: Correspondence on ‘Evaluating machine learning tools to assist title and abstract screening in systematic literature reviews: a report based on the EULAR RA Management Recommendations Task Force’ by Konzett et al.
MRI and ultrasound predictors of progression to inflammatory arthritis in anti-CCP–positive individuals with musculoskeletal symptoms without clinical synovitis: a prospective cohort study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the prevalence of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound features in anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) positive individuals with musculoskeletal symptoms without clinical synovitis (CCP+ at-risk), and compare their prognostic value for progression to inflammatory arthritis (IA). METHODS: Overall, 130 CCP+ at-risk underwent baseline contrast-enhanced 3 T MRI of the dominant/most symptomatic hand and both feet. Images were scored for synovitis, tenosynovitis, osteitis, and erosions using Rheumatoid Arthritis Magnetic Resonance Imaging Score (RAMRIS) by a rheumatologist and a radiologist. Ultrasound used a 36-joint and 18-tendon protocol for the assessment of synovitis, tenosynovitis, and bone erosions. Associations between imaging findings, clinical variables, and progression to IA were assessed using Cox models with prespecified MRI (binary and continuous score) and ultrasound (individual lesions and overall positivity) parameterisations. RESULTS: At baseline, ≥1 RAMRIS abnormality was present in all CCP+ at-risk individuals (including ultrasound-negative individuals), while ultrasound abnormalities were detected in 25.4%. Over a median follow-up of 36.5 months, 48 (36.9%) progressed to IA. Hand tenosynovitis was the only MRI feature consistently associated with progression across binary and continuous analyses. Ultrasound-detected bone erosions were the most consistently predictive ultrasound feature. A composite of MRI tenosynovitis and ultrasound-detected erosions showed an additional increase in risk, highest in individuals with both features (hazard ratio 5.83). CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort of CCP+ at-risk undergoing contemporaneous ultrasound and MRI, MRI-detected hand tenosynovitis and ultrasound bone erosions independently predicted progression to IA. Their combination identified those at the highest risk, supporting complementary roles for both modalities. The feasibility and cost-effectiveness of combined hand MRI and extensive ultrasound require evaluation.

title: Response to correspondence on ‘Frequency and characteristics of axial involvement in psoriatic arthritis: results from the International Multicentre AXIS Study’ by Luan et al
Multiomics landscape of systemic sclerosis: from autoantibody-positivity to established disease
abstract: Objectives Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a progressive autoimmune disease in which pathogenic processes may begin before clinical onset. We aimed to characterise molecular alterations across the spectrum from the asymptomatic SSc-specific autoantibody-positive (SSAP) phase through very early diagnosis of SSc (VEDOSS) to established SSc using integrated multiomics profiling. Methods In this multiomics study, we performed peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics and plasma proteomics in healthy controls, SSAP, VEDOSS, and limited and diffuse SSc. Differential expression, expression-pattern analysis across clinical groups, and functional enrichment were conducted to evaluate group-associated molecular features. Connectivity Map (CMap) analysis was used to prioritise hypothesis-generating perturbagens linked to early and persisting transcriptional signatures. Results A continuous molecular gradient was observed from health to established SSc, with SSAP and VEDOSS occupying intermediate molecular states. Immune dysregulation, particularly innate immune activation and type I interferon signalling, was detectable at the SSAP stage and showed higher activity across the ordered clinical groups. Plasma proteomics identified circulating protein markers related to vascular injury and extracellular matrix remodelling across the clinical groups. CMap analysis prioritised Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors and phosphodiesterase inhibitors as hypothesis-generating perturbagens linked to early disease-associated programmes. Conclusions Molecular abnormalities associated with SSc are detectable before overt clinical disease. Multiomics profiling identifies circulating immune, vascular-associated, and profibrotic molecular features across the SSc disease severity spectrum and provides a framework for molecular characterisation and risk stratification.

title: Ten-year outcomes after treat-to-target therapy in early rheumatoid arthritis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study is to examine 10-year clinical, structural and functional outcomes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treated with an early treat-to-target strategy, and to examine whether achievement of sustained remission in early disease is associated with favourable long-term outcomes. METHODS: The ARCTIC (Aiming for Remission in rheumatoid arthritis: a randomised trial examining the benefit of ultrasound in a Clinical TIght Control regimen) trial enrolled 230 patients with early RA and applied a strict treat-to-target strategy for 2 years. Participants were invited to a 10-year follow-up, and disease activity, radiographic damage, physical function, and survival were assessed. Patients were stratified according to achievement of sustained remission in ARCTIC and outcomes were compared between groups. RESULTS: Of the 230 patients with ARCTIC, 218 (95%) were alive at 10 years and 179 (82%) participated in the follow-up study. Eighty-two per cent of patients were in Disease Activity Score (DAS) remission 10 years after diagnosis. Radiographic progression was limited, with a median (IQR) change in total van der Heijde modified Sharp score of 2.0 (0.5, 4.5) from baseline to 10 years. Physical function and health-related quality of life improved substantially, approaching population norms. Survival was comparable to that of the general population. Patients who achieved sustained DAS remission at 2 years had lower disease activity and higher physical function at the 10-year follow-up than those who did not. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort of patients treated according to an early treat-to-target strategy, clinical, structural, and functional outcomes remained favourable at 10 years. Achievement of sustained remission in early disease was associated with higher remission rates and better physical function at 10 years. These findings support current treatment recommendations.

title: Predictive molecular signatures for successful tapering of canakinumab in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Canakinumab induces clinical remission in a substantial proportion of patients with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA), although not all achieve a complete response. However, tapering and withdrawal frequently lead to disease flares. This study aimed to identify serum and transcriptomic biomarkers that predict successful or unsuccessful tapering of canakinumab in sJIA. METHODS: Seventy-nine patients with sJIA in remission on canakinumab enrolled in a randomised withdrawal study were analysed; 71 had samples available for gene expression profiling. Serum biomarkers were quantified using Luminex assays. Whole-blood RNA was assessed by RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) and a targeted 67-gene NanoString panel informed by exploratory analyses. Differential expression, hierarchical clustering, and enrichment analyses were performed. Biomarkers and gene signatures were compared between patients who later successfully withdrew canakinumab and those who experienced unsuccessful tapering. RESULTS: Lower serum levels of sCD163, CXCL9, interleukin (IL)-1RA, and IL-18 were associated with successful tapering. RNA-Seq showed marked differences between active and inactive sJIA and revealed that future nonresponders exhibited lower expression of type I IFN-induced and higher expression of erythopoiesis-related genes. NanoString profiling identified 9 genes (ATF6, BCL6, FAS, IL1B, MAPK1, PPARG, SLC25A37, TNFAIP3, and UBE2D1) overexpressed in patients with unsuccessful tapering, reflecting persistent inflammation and cellular stress. A composite score of these genes discriminated successful from unsuccessful discontinuation (area under curve, AUC, 0.71). CONCLUSIONS: Serum inflammatory markers and targeted gene expression signatures identify patients with sJIA at higher risk of flare during canakinumab tapering. Combined molecular biomarker profiling may enable individualised tapering strategies and support precision medicine approaches for Still's disease.

title: Estimating 2-year risk of first relapse in ANCA-associated vasculitis: derivation of a risk-prediction model based on participants in the PEXIVAS trial
abstract: Objectives Individuals with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) differ in their risk of relapse. Estimation of an individual's risk may inform decision-making around monitoring and treatment. Methods We performed a post hoc analysis of participants with AAV with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 2 or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage enrolled in a trial assessing the effects of plasma exchange and a reduced glucocorticoid dosing regimen who achieved disease remission. We estimated the risk of first relapse within 2 years of remission. We first identified candidate predictors from the literature. Candidate predictors measured in our data set and associated with relapse within 2 years of remission underwent further selection using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression and time-to-event analysis. Model stability was assessed with variable inclusion, multiple shrinkage methods, and VanderWeele's E. Model discrimination was assessed using concordance statistics, and calibration using the slope. Results We included data from 649 trial participants, of whom 100 experienced a relapse within 2 years of remission. The final risk estimation model included sex, use of oral cyclophosphamide or rituximab as induction agent, ANCA subtype, nonhaemorrhagic respiratory involvement or mucous membrane/eye involvement at presentation, and eGFR at remission. The optimism-corrected Harrell's area under the receiver-operator curve 0.709 (95% CI 0.707-0.710). The calibration slope was 0.99 (95% CI 0.65-1.34). Conclusions Our model estimates the risk of first relapse for individuals with AAV within 2 years after achieving disease remission. This may inform monitoring and treatment decisions. The model will benefit from future external validation.

title: HOXD13 links positional identity to primary cilia–dependent signalling in synovial fibroblasts
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Homeobox (HOX) transcription factors establish positional identity along the embryonic body axis, yet their functional roles in adult tissues remain poorly understood. METHODS: Synovial fibroblasts (SFs) and synovial tissue from rheumatoid arthritis (RA), osteoarthritis (OA), and noninflammatory donors were analysed using transcriptomic, epigenetic, and functional approaches. HOXD10, HOXD11, and HOXD13 were silenced in primary SFs, followed by RNA sequencing, gene set enrichment analysis, and assessment of proliferation, cell-cycle progression, and DNA damage responses. Primary cilia were assessed by immunofluorescence in SFs, and cilia-dependent Hedgehog signalling was evaluated using a GLI luciferase reporter assay. RESULTS: HOXD10, HOXD11, and HOXD13 were selectively expressed in SFs from distal joints. We identify epigenetic mechanisms that maintain the anatomically restricted expression of these genes in adult SFs. Silencing of 5' HOXDs induces transcriptional changes in SFs that mirror joint-specific differences observed in RA. Notably, HOXD13 emerges as a key regulator of primary cilia function, influencing cell-cycle control and DNA damage responses, and genome stability. Consistent with these findings, we uncover joint-specific differences in primary cilia morphology, cell-cycle regulation, and DNA damage repair capacity in SFs. CONCLUSIONS: Our results identify a previously unrecognised role for HOXD13 in linking embryonic positional identity to adult stromal cell function through primary cilia-dependent pathways. We propose that HOXD13-mediated regulation of primary cilia contributes to joint-specific SF phenotypes, providing a mechanistic framework linking positional identity to anatomically distinct fibroblast states. These findings suggest that developmental patterning genes can shape site-specific inflammatory responses.

title: BAFF-APRIL blockade reveals isotype-specific pathogenic autoantibody remodelling in antiphospholipid syndrome
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Durable suppression of pathogenic autoantibodies remains a central challenge in antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases. We aimed to examine pathogenic autoantibody remodelling under targeted humoral immunotherapy using antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) as a tractable human model. METHODS: In this study, we used dual blockade of B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) with telitacicept as an immune perturbation in a high-risk triple-positive antiphospholipid antibody (aPL) cohort including primary APS and asymptomatic aPL carriers, integrating longitudinal serology with paired pretreatment and posttreatment peripheral-blood and bone marrow single-cell and B-cell receptor repertoire profiling. RESULTS: Telitacicept induced broad B-lineage contraction but remodelled aPL responses nonuniformly, with consistent immunoglobulin (Ig) M- and IgA-class reductions and heterogeneous IgG-class suppression. This pattern coincided with extensive peripheral B-cell and plasmablast turnover, but greater clonal continuity within class-switched marrow plasma cells. In an exploratory post-hoc analysis of baseline IgG aPL-positive patients, incomplete IgG suppression was associated with greater persistence of pretreatment immunoglobulin heavy constant gamma positive (IGHG⁺) clonotypes and associated secretory programmes, whereas residual marrow IGHG⁺ plasma-cell abundance did not clearly distinguish response groups. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these findings define compartment- and isotype-selective remodelling of pathogenic autoantibody responses in APS and identify persistent marrow IGHG⁺ plasma-cell clonotypes as a cellular correlate of incomplete suppression of IgG aPL.

title: DNA methylation signatures distinguish gout from asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and converge with genetic risk at immune-metabolic loci
abstract: Objectives Why only a minority of hyperuricaemic individuals develop gout remains unclear, and epigenetic differences between these states are poorly characterised. We aimed to define DNA methylation signatures distinguishing gout from asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and evaluate their utility for molecular stratification. Methods We conducted a 2-stage case-control epigenetic study of gout (n = 124), asymptomatic hyperuricaemia (n = 121), and normouricaemic controls (n = 124). Peripheral-blood DNA methylation was profiled by genome-wide targeted bisulphite sequencing in a discovery cohort (n = 83), integrating differentially methylated regions (DMRs) and cytosines (DMCs) with genome-wide association study loci and transcription-factor binding sites (TFBSs). Candidate signatures were then tested by targeted amplicon methylation sequencing in an independent cohort (n = 286), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator logistic regression constructed methylation-only and epigenetic-clinical classifiers. Results DMRs were identified across all 3 pairwise comparisons of gout, hyperuricaemia, and normouricaemic controls, mapping to 84 genes that overlapped gout/serum urate risk loci—including HLA-DRB1, TAP2 , and GNAS —and were enriched at TFBSs, with ZNF571 linked to IL27 and SAA2 . One hundred thirteen DMCs were validated and used to build classifiers: a methylation-only model distinguished gout from normouricaemic controls (test-set area under the curve 0.96) and outperformed clinical variables in gout vs nongout controls (0.91 vs 0.78; DeLong P = 0.032), while integrating methylation with clinical variables improved the most challenging distinction—gout vs asymptomatic hyperuricaemia—from 0.67 to 0.87 (DeLong P = 0.018). Conclusions Peripheral-blood DNA methylation captures reproducible, stage-specific differences across gout, hyperuricaemia, and normouricaemic states converging with immune-metabolic genetic risk. These signatures support methylation-based molecular stratification, although prospective validation is needed before clinical deployment.Unlabelled box dummy alt text •Hyperuricaemia is necessary for gout, but only a minority of people with elevated serum urate develop clinical disease, so factors beyond urate must govern progression. •Gout- and serum urate–associated genetic loci explain only part of disease risk, and many lie in noncoding regions with unclear regulatory effects. •DNA methylation changes have been reported at selected gout-related genes, but no genome-wide methylation signature distinguishing gout from asymptomatic hyperuricaemia has been established. •A 2-stage study identified reproducible peripheral-blood DNA methylation signatures that distinguish gout, asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, and normouricaemic states. •These signatures overlapped with established gout and serum urate genetic risk loci, converged on antigen presentation and metabolic pathways, and were enriched at transcription-factor binding sites. •A methylation-only classifier separated gout from normouricaemic controls with high accuracy, and adding methylation to routine clinical variables most improved the clinically hardest distinction—gout vs asymptomatic hyperuricaemia—where serum urate is uninformative, indicating that methylation carries diagnostic information independent of urate. •The convergence of methylation with genetic risk loci motivates integrated genotype-methylation (eg, methylation quantitative trait loci) and functional studies to test whether these changes are causal in the transition from hyperuricaemia to gout. •Methylation-based markers could refine molecular stratification of urate-related disease beyond serum urate, particularly in separating gout from asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, and may aid trial enrichment or targeted surveillance.

title: Correspondence on ‘Enhancing diagnostic accuracy in axial spondyloarthritis through centralised clinical and imaging evaluation’ by Poddubnyy et al
Immune reset in rheumatic autoimmune disease: from a tantalising metaphor to a measurable therapeutic state
abstract: Immune reset is increasingly invoked to describe the possibility that a one-off intervention is able to produce durable treatment-free control of rheumatic autoimmune diseases. However, the term remains imprecise and is often conflated with lymphodepletion or immune reconstitution. We argue that immune reset should denote a persistently normalised therapeutic state rather than an inferred consequence of profound immunodepletion. A credible immune reset claim should require sustained off-therapy clinical control beyond the expected pharmacodynamic window, stabilisation or improvement of the involved organs, and demonstrable reconfiguration of disease-relevant immune circuits in blood and accessible tissue. Importantly, restoration of immune competence, including protective immunoglobulins, vaccine responsiveness, and host defence against infection, is an essential part of immune reset. Naïve B-cell repopulation, serological improvement, repertoire rejuvenation, or transient clinical remission alone are insufficient to document immune reset because pathogenic compartments, irreversible organ damage, and acquired immune deficiency may persist. Until validated prospectively, the concept of immune reset should remain a hypothetical construct or perhaps a clinical aspiration rather than a therapeutic reality across treatment modalities and autoimmune disease entities.

title: Preclinical and clinical outcomes in patients with high rheumatoid factor levels treated with TNF inhibitors:a systematic review
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Rheumatoid factor (RF) binds to the fragment crystallisable (Fc) portion of immunoglobulin G1 and can also bind to the Fc region of biologic agents, forming immune complexes that are subsequently cleared by macrophages, contributing to reduced drug availability and diminished therapeutic response. In this systematic review, we examined the binding mechanism and impact of RF on tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFis) with and without an Fc portion, along with the impact of RF levels on drug concentration and clinical outcomes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). METHODS: Searches were carried out in MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL up to January 2025 and updated in July 2025. Abstracts and full texts were screened, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Studies that included at least 1 group of adult patients with high RF treated with TNFis (with or without an Fc region) with outcomes of interest were considered for inclusion. RESULTS: Of the 21 studies included, 1 study reported both clinical and preclinical data, 3 studies reported preclinical data, and 18 studies reported efficacy and effectiveness outcomes in 8910 patients treated with TNFis. Clinical endpoints, such as the Clinical Disease Activity Index, the Simple Disease Activity Index, the Disease Activity Score-28 with C-reactive protein (DAS28-CRP), or erythrocyte sedimentation rate (DAS28-ESR), and Boolean remission were similar or slightly better in patients with high RF who received Fc-free TNFis, relative to those with low RF levels. CONCLUSIONS: Considering these observations, Fc-free TNFis may provide some advantages to RA patients with high RF levels.

title: Early arthritis signs and symptoms revisited—is synovitis what we are assessing?
authors: Annette H. M. van der Helm-van Mil
abstract: Classic signs of joint inflammation at physical examination of patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are joint swelling and joint tenderness. In the hand, additional characteristic signs include a positive squeeze test, reduced grip strength, and incomplete fist closure. Typical symptoms that are presumed to be inflammatory are pain and morning stiffness. Traditionally, these signs and symptoms have been thought to reflect underlying synovitis, ie, inflammation of the intra-articular synovial lining. Over the past 15 years, however, we have recognised the involvement of other inflamed tissues, such as tenosynovitis and osteitis, and more recently, interosseous tendon inflammation in the hand, and intermetatarsal bursitis in the forefoot. The question now arises as to whether the signs and symptoms observed during clinical assessment of RA are purely driven by synovitis, or if, and to what extent, they can be explained by other inflamed tissues. Therefore, we have summarised the current literature to explain which inflamed tissues contribute to the clinical characteristics in early arthritis, as well as during the at-risk stage of clinically suspect arthralgia. We found that signs and symptoms are not only explained by synovitis, but also by inflammation of tendon sheaths and intermetatarsal bursae. Among these different inflamed tissues, tenosynovitis most frequently contributed to classic clinical characteristics. Other inflamed tissues, eg, interosseous tendon inflammation and intermetatarsal bursitis, seemed to have a smaller contribution. Together, the findings provide a revisited but advanced understanding of early arthritis signs and symptoms: they arise not only from synovitis, but also from various inflamed tissues.

title: IgG4-related disease is not associated with an increased incidence of malignancy in a large, single-centre cohort
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a systemic, immune-mediated disease-causing inflammation and fibrosis in multiple organs, often associated with elevated serum IgG4 concentrations. Whether IgG4-RD is associated with malignancy remains unclear. We investigated whether there is an association between IgG4-RD and incident malignancy. METHODS: We performed a single-centre, retrospective cohort study of patients who fulfilled the American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology IgG4-RD Classification Criteria. Malignancy history was collected by survey and medical record review. Age- and sex-stratified malignancy incidence rates in the cohort were compared with rates in the general US population. Cox proportional hazards were used to identify disease characteristics associated with incident malignancy. RESULTS: Of the 348 patients with IgG4-RD in our cohort, 34 (10%) developed incident malignancies over a median follow-up of 8.04 years (IQR, 1.35-14.72 years). The most common malignancies were lymphoma (n = 6, 16% of malignancies), prostate cancer (n = 6, 16%), and lung cancer (n = 5, 13%). Compared with the general US population, there was no increased incidence of malignancy in patients with IgG4-RD (standardised incidence ratio, 0.88 [0.61-1.23]). Among patients with IgG4-RD, those who ever smoked (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 2.46 [1.16-5.24]) or were older (HR, 1.35 [1.00-1.83] per decade) had increased risk of malignancy, whereas female patients (HR, 0.37 [0.14-0.96]) and those with submandibular gland involvement (HR, 0.25 [0.10-0.61]) had decreased risk. CONCLUSIONS: IgG4-RD was not associated with an increased incidence of malignancy following IgG4-RD onset. Among patients with IgG4-RD, smoking and older age at IgG4-RD onset were associated with higher malignancy risk. Female sex and submandibular gland involvement were associated with lower malignancy risk.

title: Correspondence on ‘Teclistamab induces rapid clinical response and deep tissue depletion in refractory systemic sclerosis—a case series’ by Siegert et al
Response to a Correspondence on ‘Teclistamab induces rapid clinical response and deep tissue depletion in refractory systemic sclerosis – a case series’
The ASAS core set for the assessment of axial spondyloarthritis in clinical practice
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) core set for the assessment of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) in clinical practice. This entails defining an internationally endorsed and clinically feasible guiding set of domains and corresponding instruments that considers both the assessment scenarios of 'routine' and 'extended' outpatient visits. METHODS: A scoping literature review and Delphi survey among stakeholders (ASAS members, non-ASAS member rheumatologists, and patients) informed the selection of clinically relevant domains and instruments for the core set. The selected domains and instruments were presented and discussed with the ASAS community at the 2026 ASAS annual meeting, and voted upon for endorsement. RESULTS: Following discussion with the ASAS community, the core set was endorsed by a majority of ASAS members. Five domains are included for routine visits: 'disease activity', 'pain', 'peripheral manifestations', 'extra-musculoskeletal manifestations', and 'treatment aspects', with 1 instrument recommended for each domain, alongside several optional instruments. Four supplementary domains are included for extended visits (to be assessed in addition to all routine visit domains): 'structural damage', 'overall functioning and health', 'comorbidities', and 'mobility', with at least 1 recommended or optional instrument incorporated for each domain. CONCLUSIONS: The ASAS core set for the assessment of axSpA in clinical practice represents the minimum domains to be systematically assessed in all patients during routine and extended visits, with corresponding instruments. Its development marks a step towards improved standardisation of disease assessments in axSpA in the clinical setting, providing a practical framework that aligns with existing management recommendations.

title: Sustained improvement of systemic lupus erythematosus‑associated pulmonary arterial hypertension by CD19 CAR T-cell therapy: 1‑year haemodynamic follow‑up
Type I interferon activation in classical monocytes and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells characterises the ultrasound-negative phase of imminent rheumatoid arthritis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a prototypical autoimmune disease, characterised by prolonged systemic autoimmunity before organ-specific tissue inflammation. Understanding immune mechanisms that drive the transition from systemic autoimmunity to joint-specific pathology is key to arthritis prevention. In this study, we define immune signatures in anticitrullinated protein antibodies-positive (ACPA+) at-risk individuals who imminently progress to RA, comparing those with and without ultrasound (US)-detectable subclinical synovitis. METHODS: We performed single‑cell RNA sequencing and proteomic profiling on prospectively collected blood samples from high-risk ACPA+ imminent progressors (n = 22), who were further stratified by the presence or absence of US-detectable subclinical synovitis and compared them with ACPA+ nonprogressors (n=18). RESULTS: We found type I interferon (IFN-I) upregulation in peripheral CD14+ classical monocyte and Granzyme K protein (GZMK)+ CD8+ T cells in US-negative (USneg, n = 11) imminent progressors. In contrast, US-positive (USpos, n = 11) progressors exhibited a phenotypic shift in CD14+ classical monocytes towards interleukin 1 beta (IL1ß)+ expression and clonal expansion of GZMB+ cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. GZMB+ and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells were largely clonotypically distinct. Plasma proteomics also revealed a shift from Toll-like receptor-associated innate pathways in USneg progressors towards effector and tissue-remodelling signatures in USpos progressors. CONCLUSIONS: In ACPA+ high-risk individuals, IFN-I-driven activation of peripheral innate CD14+ classical monocytes and GZMK+ CD8+ T cell subsets occur before the onset of subclinical synovitis when RA is imminent. Distinct inflammatory and effector programmes, including GZMB+ CD8+ T cells clonal expansion, are associated with the onset of subclinical synovitis.

title: Emerging drugs in phase 2/3 and selected phase 1/2 cellular-therapy trials: a glimpse into the future of systemic sclerosis treatment
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease that affects multiple organs. SSc is associated with the highest mortality rate among rheumatic diseases and significantly diminishes quality of life. Consequently, research efforts have focused on understanding its etiopathogenesis and on developing related targeted therapies. Over the past decade, organ-specific therapies (such as tocilizumab and nintedanib for lung fibrosis) have been introduced to manage various manifestations of SSc. However, there is a lack of approved therapies for the overall disease. Currently, many novel compounds are being further evaluated in ongoing clinical trials. This article reviews drugs currently in phase 2 and phase 3 trials and highlights the key disease mechanisms they target in SSc. Recent advances in understanding the pathogenesis of SSc have facilitated the identification of actionable molecular and cellular pathways, leading to the testing of targeted therapeutic strategies. Concurrently, increasing emphasis is being placed on patient stratification and personalised treatment approaches to optimise clinical trial design, improve treatment responsiveness, and enhance the generalisability of trial outcomes. Among emerging treatments, cellular therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, represent a significant innovation. This paradigm shift offers substantial potential for improving outcomes in systemic sclerosis.

title: Ten rules to reduce noise and increase precision in imaging studies in rheumatology: a methodological viewpoint informed by narrative reviews
abstract: Imaging studies are ubiquitous in rheumatology. Research in imaging has throughout the years mainly focused on improving the sensitivity of imaging techniques and scoring methods. Remarkably little attention has been paid to constraining unwarranted noise (acquisition, measurement, and analytical error) in spite of strict regulatory guidance about noise reduction for new drug approval. Noise reduction in imaging depends on the application of several methodological rules. Scientific credibility of imaging results should not depend on the complexity and incomprehensibility of the reported statistical model (plus eye-catching P values), but rather on optimal signal-to-noise ratio, usually meaning less 'noise' at a given 'signal'. This viewpoint deals with noise reduction. Repeated scoring of existing images, correction of inappropriate prior scoring, correction of fallible previous analytical procedures and more, can all contribute to a more trustworthy and better result. In the current world of patient-reported clinical information, imaging data still stand out as being rather 'objective'. But the influence of scoring and analysis in terms of unwarranted noise by readers and data analysts cannot be disregarded. This viewpoint proposes 10 expert-based rules for noise reduction at the level of image scoring, database handling, and data analysis. These rules should be considered not-yet-validated methodological hypotheses that require empirical validation through comparative methodological research.

title: Medicalising the Human Cell Atlas for musculoskeletal disease: towards a translational roadmap
abstract: The Human Cell Atlas (HCA) has fundamentally changed the way biologists describe human tissues. However, its greatest promise for musculoskeletal (MSK) practitioners lies ahead: to convert cellular maps into clinically actionable knowledge. MSK diseases are common, heterogeneous, and often insufficiently stratified by current diagnostic labels. The same label, such as rheumatoid arthritis, can conceal distinct cellular mechanisms, tissue niches, and therapeutic vulnerabilities. Conversely, apparently different disorders such as tendinopathy or fibrotic capsulitis can share convergent stromal, immune, vascular, or neuronal programmes. A MSK-HCA therefore should not be conceived as a passive reference catalogue. It should be 'medicalised': designed from the outset to connect tissue atlases with clinical phenotypes, imaging, biospecimens, genetic risk, biomarkers, perturbation experiments, and interventional trials. In this review, we describe how single-cell, single-nucleus, spatial, and multiomic approaches are beginning to map MSK tissues from development to ageing and from health to disease. We highlight examples in embryonic skeletal development, bone marrow, muscle ageing, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, tendon disease, and inflammatory fibrosis and show how these data can reframe disease taxonomy around pathogenic cell states rather than organ-level labels alone. We propose a translational roadmap in which atlases define healthy reference coordinates, identify disease-enriched cell states, nominate biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and then learn from clinical trial outcomes. For clinicians, the MSK-HCA offers a route to mechanism-led diagnosis and patient stratification; for scientists, it provides a shared coordinate system for testing how genes, cells, and tissue microenvironments generate disease. Medicalising the HCA could make cellular medicine a practical foundation for precision rheumatology and regenerative MSK therapy.

title: Kidney spatial multiomics mapping decodes scleroderma renal crisis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) is a life-threatening complication of systemic sclerosis with incompletely understood pathogenesis, hindering therapeutics development and contributing to high rates of end-stage kidney disease and mortality. We aimed to construct a spatially resolved cellular and molecular atlas of SRC kidneys to identify disease-specific microenvironments and therapeutic targets. METHODS: Kidney biopsy samples from 12 patients with SRC manifesting histopathologically as thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), 6 patients with lupus nephritis (LN), and 3 normal kidneys were analysed by spatial transcriptomics (discovery cohort), and the findings were validated in an expanded cohort by multiplexed imaging. Spatial organization and cellular phenotypes were analysed across histopathologically defined regions. RESULTS: Multiplexed imaging demonstrated a pathological triad of TMA, immune infiltration, and fibrotic remodelling in SRC kidneys. SRC and LN shared activation of the complement cascade, type I interferon signalling, and fibrotic remodelling. However, SRC exhibited a distinct vascular-hypoxic axis. Spatial analyses revealed disease-specific glomerular niches at the interface between renal parenchymal cells and prominent myeloid immune cells. We demonstrated dynamic molecular signatures that progressed from mild lesions through overt SRC-associated pathological changes (glomerular TMA or arterial injury) to chronic lesions in each histopathologically defined region. Multiple pathological pathways were already upregulated in mild lesions, with selective enrichment in glomerular TMA and arterial injury, ultimately converging on injury and remodelling programmes in the chronic lesions. CONCLUSIONS: This study advances our understanding of SRC beyond histopathology to the molecular and cellular landscape, providing an omics-driven framework to accelerate therapeutic target discovery in this rare, devastating disease.

title: A CCL20+ macrophage subpopulation is the major producer of TNF in axial spondyloarthritis synovium and is driven by CD40L and a myeloid autocrine circuit
abstract: Objectives Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin (IL)-17 are central drivers of axial spondyloarthritis (AxSpA). We previously identified activated CD4+ tissue-resident memory Th17 cells as the principal source of IL-17A/F in AxSpA synovium. We sought to define the cellular source of TNF and mechanisms driving the CCL20 + myeloid phenotype in joint and blood. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of synovial tissue from 5 patients with AxSpA was combined with immunofluorescence, synovial-fluid scRNA-seq, and flow cytometry, as well as comparisons with rheumatoid arthritis datasets. Monocyte-derived macrophages from healthy controls (HCs) and patients with AxSpA were cocultured with activated autologous CD4 + T cells, with blocking and cytokine experiments defining mechanisms of CCL20 + induction. Circulating monocytes were assessed by scRNA-seq and functional assays. Results CCL20 + macrophages were the predominant source of TNF in AxSpA synovium, with TNF protein confirmed in tissue and synovial fluid. Activated CD4 + T cells induced the CCL20 + phenotype through CD40L-CD40 signalling and an IL-1β/TNF-α autocrine circuit in HC-derived and AxSpA-derived cells. Baseline AxSpA monocytes showed a higher CCL20 + signature than HC monocytes, but this difference largely disappeared after T-cell-mediated induction. Under stimulation, AxSpA monocytes also produced more TNF, IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-23 than HC monocytes, a difference attenuated following IL-1/TNF priming. Conclusions CCL20 + macrophages are a major CD40L- and IL-1β/TNF-α-driven source of TNF in AxSpA synovium. AxSpA circulating monocytes exhibit heightened basal CCL20 + signatures and inflammatory responsiveness that converge towards HC responses after inflammatory priming, supporting circulating CCL20 + monocytes as a marker of IL-1β/TNF-α-driven myeloid inflammation.

title: International recommendations for the use of imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of polymyalgia rheumatica
abstract: Objectives The study aims to develop international recommendations for the use of imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). Methods An international, multidisciplinary task force of 30 members from 12 countries was convened; the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology standard operating procedures were followed. Six clinical key questions addressing the role of imaging (ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography) in diagnosis, monitoring, outcome prediction, and technical aspects in PMR were the basis for a systematic literature review. Recommendations were formulated based on evidence and expert opinion and refined iteratively until consensus was achieved. The level of agreement was assessed by voting. Results Three overarching principles and 7 recommendations were developed. PMR remains primarily a clinical diagnosis. Imaging is neither required to confirm PMR in patients with a high clinical probability of the disease nor to exclude PMR in case of low clinical probability. Imaging is most useful in patients with intermediate pretest probability (ie, atypical presentations or suspected alternative/overlapping conditions). No single imaging modality demonstrated sufficient accuracy to be recommended as a first-line test; therefore, imaging should be individualised according to clinical presentation, differential diagnoses, access, and local expertise. Vascular imaging should be performed when overlap with giant cell arteritis is suspected, whereas systematic screening for subclinical vasculitis is not supported by current evidence. Utilising imaging for disease monitoring or outcome prediction is currently not recommended. Conclusions These recommendations provide the first evidence-based guidance for the use of imaging in PMR, reinforcing clinical assessment as the cornerstone of diagnosis and positioning imaging as a context-driven adjunct.

title: Performance of MRI-based synthetic CT for detecting spinal new bone formation in patients with inflammatory arthritis and healthy controls: a comparison with MRI, CT, and radiography
abstract: Objectives This study aims to compare magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based synthetic computed tomography (sCT), T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (T1wMRI), low-dose CT (ldCT), and radiography for detecting spinal new bone formation (NBF) in participants with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and healthy controls (HCs). Methods All participants underwent whole-spine ldCT and MRI in addition to cervical/lumbar spine radiography (not HCs). sCT was reconstructed using BoneMRI. Images were independently assessed for NBF by 2 readers blinded to other imaging and clinical information. One reader repeated ldCT and sCT reads after 6 months. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated using ldCT as the reference standard. Inter-reader and intra-reader reliability were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Cohen's kappa. Results Sixty-nine participants (36 males, mean age 51.4 years) were included: 30 axSpA, 19 PsA, 10 RA, and 10 HCs. The mean number of NBFs per participant was 25.8 on ldCT, 24.0 on sCT, 9.3 on T1wMRI, and 6.9 on radiography. Sensitivity for NBF detection was highest for sCT (70%), followed by radiography (50% cervical/lumbar and 21% whole-spine) and T1wMRI (28%); specificity was ≥93% across modalities. Inter-reader reliability was high for sCT and ldCT (excellent ICCs, substantial kappas), whereas radiography and T1wMRI showed good ICCs with substantial/moderate kappas. Intra-reader reliability and inter-modality agreement for sCT and ldCT were excellent/substantial (ICCs/kappas). Conclusions Using ldCT as a reference standard, sCT demonstrated substantially higher sensitivity than T1wMRI and radiography. Intra- and inter-reader reliability and inter-modality agreement between ldCT and sCT were comparable, suggesting that discrepancies in lesion detection primarily reflect reader variability rather than inter-modality differences.

title: Real‑world assessment of the effectiveness and response profiles of biologic DMARDs in psoriatic arthritis: findings from an emulated multicentre clinical trial
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate 6-month effectiveness and long-term drug-retention rates of biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) using real-world data analysed within an emulated multicentre clinical trial framework. Secondary objectives included the characterisation of response profiles and the identification of possible predictors of clinical response across bDMARD classes. METHODS: Between January 2022 and June 2025, consecutive patients with moderate-to-high PsA disease activity initiating a bDMARD were prospectively enrolled in a multicentre Gruppo Italiano di Ricerca in Reumatologia Clinica e Sperimentale study. Real-world data were analysed within a target trial emulation framework comparing tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, interleukin (IL)-17 inhibitors, and IL-23-pathway inhibitors. Propensity score weighting was used to improve comparability in measured baseline characteristics across treatment groups. Effectiveness was assessed through longitudinal changes in the Disease Activity Index for Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA) over 6 months. Subsequent long-term drug retention was evaluated using a 6-month landmark analysis restricted to patients who remained on the index bDMARD at month 6. Potential clinical factors associated with treatment response and discontinuation were also explored. RESULTS: Overall, 990 patients were included: 342 initiated TNF inhibitors, 313 IL-17 inhibitors, and 335 IL-23-pathway inhibitors. DAPSA decreased significantly over 6 months in all 3 treatment groups, with no statistically significant between-class differences in adjusted longitudinal trajectories. Among patients who remained on the index bDMARD through month 6, the adjusted analyses did not identify statistically significant between-class differences in subsequent long-term drug retention. Shorter disease duration was associated with more favourable outcomes in selected exploratory analyses, whereas associations with previous bDMARD exposure were inconsistent. Additional class-specific associations were identified but should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Adverse-event-related discontinuations documented in routine clinical records were described; however, the study was not designed to support formal comparative safety conclusions. CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world emulated multicentre clinical trial, bDMARDs showed comparable overall trajectories of short-term effectiveness and long-term treatment persistence in PsA. The identification of partially distinct response patterns may support a more individualised approach to bDMARD selection.

title: Practical recommendations for revaccination following BCMA-targeted therapies in adult patients with autoimmune diseases
abstract: Objectives B-cell-directed immune-reset therapies are emerging as transformative approaches in autoimmune diseases, but their impact on long-term humoral immunity remains uncertain. These strategies encompass a broad range of B-cell targets and therapeutic modalities, the most clinically established targets include CD19, CD20, and B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), with T-cell-redirecting approaches, particularly chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies and bispecific T-cell engagers, among the most validated modalities. Here, we aim to provide a practical framework for revaccination in patients with autoimmune diseases. Methods We examine existing clinical evidence on the effects of BCMA-targeting therapies with respect to antivaccine titres to provide a revaccination framework in autoimmunity. Results Current clinical evidence suggests that BCMA-targeting therapies reduce vaccine-specific antibody titres along with total immunoglobulin levels. Insights from oncology studies provide a framework for understanding antivaccine responses in the context of profound BCMA-directed cell depletion, with the caveat that important differences exist between patients with autoimmunity and those with malignancies, including the magnitude and duration of immunosuppressive treatment. Conclusions We propose a pragmatic revaccination approach after BCMA-targeting therapies in adult patients with autoimmune diseases, utilising minimal serologic monitoring. Future studies of these novel drugs will refine our understanding of the optimal timing and need for revaccinations in this population.

title: Correspondence on ‘Spacing of a TNF inhibitor or dose reduction of methotrexate vs continued treatment in patients with rheumatoid arthritis in remission or low disease activity (SORAIRO trial)’ by Imai et al

Response to correspondence on ‘Spacing of a TNF inhibitor or dose reduction of methotrexate vs continued treatment in patients with rheumatoid arthritis in remission or low disease activity (SORAIRO trial)’
Interleukin 4-receptor-α blockade in localised scleroderma: a phase 2 proof-of-concept study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: 2 signature. In preclinical mouse models, development of fibrosis critically depends on IL-4/signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6). Yet, the role of IL-4/IL-13 in human fibrosing diseases remains unknown, and treatment development requires a deeper understanding of the role of IL-4/IL-13 in the pathogenesis. The local inflammation and the development of fibrosis in localised scleroderma (LS) are similar to those in systemic sclerosis and other fibrosing diseases. METHODS: In this article, we investigated the role of IL-4/IL-13 signalling in LS in a randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT04200755). We studied the effect of 6 months of blocking IL-4-receptor α with dupilumab on disease progression, sclerosis-associated inflammation, and sclerosis-specific gene expression. RESULTS: Already this short-term intervention resulted in a significant clinical improvement over placebo, a significant attenuation of the local inflammation, a specific and significant reduction of the IL-4/IL-13-dependent gene signature, and a partial suppression of genes coding for fibrosis-inducing proteins. CONCLUSIONS: Thus, selective inhibition of IL-4/IL-13 prevents the progression of LS and is promising for therapeutic prevention of other fibrosing diseases.

title: Rescue therapy of paediatric lupus nephritis with plasma cell-directed antibodies
Spatial transcriptomics in immune-mediated necrotising myopathy uncovers a specific necrotic signature related to immune-driven fibrosis
abstract: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathies (IMNM) are characterised by muscle fibre necrosis, complement deposits around non-necrotic fibres, and macrophage infiltrates. Patients experience muscle damage with fibro-fatty replacement, leading to poor strength recovery, but the pathogenesis remains unclear. To investigate IMNM pathogenesis, we applied spatial transcriptomics on myositis muscle biopsies and integrated the results with published single-nucleus transcriptomic data. This combined approach enabled analysis of gene expression with spatial localisation in the muscle. Inflammatory, fibrotic, regenerative, and lipid metabolism-related signatures were identified in IMNM, distinct from other myositis, with specific distribution in necrotic and peri-necrotic regions. A unique subtype of immune-driven fibroblasts expressing SFRP4 was enriched in IMNM necrotic areas. These cells carried a strong proportion of IMNM-enriched pathological signatures, notably a complement-linked 'tumour-like' inflammatory fibroblast signature and a specific interferon response, characterised by the expression of metallothioneins. Peri-necrotic areas were characterised by pathological muscle signatures carrying interferon response and FABP4+ metabolically dysfunctional signatures. In conclusion, IMNM necrotic muscle areas are linked to a specific SFRP4-expressing fibroblast subtype interacting with macrophages, potentially driving the pathological muscle phenotype and contributing to inflammation, fibro-fatty replacement, and strength loss.

title: Mosunetuzumab as salvage therapy for refractory connective tissue diseases: clinical responses and immunological insights
Proinflammatory strains of Mediterraneibacter gnavus are enriched during spondyloarthritis and bolster disease severity in animal model
abstract: Objectives Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatism with osteoarticular and extra‑articular manifestations. Intestinal dysbiosis has been implicated in SpA, notably the expansion of Mediterraneibacter gnavus (MG), a gram-positive coccus associated with several inflammatory disorders. We aimed to determine whether distinct MG strains were associated with SpA and contributed to disease pathogenesis. Methods MG strains from patients with SpA and healthy controls (HCs) were identified based on metagenomic analysis, isolated and whole‑genome sequenced. Pathogenicity of selected strains was compared by mono-associating curdlan-treated germ‑free SpA-prone SKG mice. Putative strain selection under inflammatory pressure was examined by culturing MG in the presence of nitric oxide (NO). Functional effects were assessed by exposing monocytes from patients with SpA to MGstrains. Results Phylogenetic analysis separated MG strains into 3 main clades/subclades, using both metagenomic data and sequencing of 46 MG strains (39 from SpA and 7 from HCs). SpA-derived strains were significantly enriched in 2 clades/subclades, whereas the third clade was dominated by strains from HCs, suggesting clade-specific disease association. MG-mono-association of curdlan-treated SKG mice induced SpA, in which SpA-derived strains induced stronger colonic inflammation and arthritis. Consistently, MG DNA of these strains persisted in the inflamed colonic submucosa and SpA-derived strains showed enhanced resistance to NO. In vitro SpA-derived strains were enriched in toxic and proinflammatory properties. Conclusions SpA is associated with a distinct repertoire of MG strains characterised by increased adaptability to inflammatory stress and heightened proinflammatory and toxic potential. These findings establish a link between strain‑level microbial diversity and disease susceptibility.

title: Nicotinamide N-methyltransferase drives fibroblast activation and skin fibrosis in systemic sclerosis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is characterised by persistent fibroblast activation and progressive extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation. The mechanisms sustaining profibrotic fibroblast states remain poorly understood. Nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), a S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-consuming enzyme that modulates cellular methylation potential, has been implicated in fibrotic tissue remodelling. In this study, we investigated the role of NNMT in dermal fibroblast (DF) activation and fibrosis in SSc. METHODS: Bulk RNA-sequencing (RNA-Seq), single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics datasets from SSc skin were analysed. Primary human DFs were subjected to small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated NNMT knockdown or pharmacological NNMT inhibition followed by transcriptomic, metabolomic, epigenetic, and functional profiling. Downstream transcription factors were assessed by QuantSeq 3' RNA-Seq following activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), SRY-box transcription factor (SOX9), and serum response factor (SRF) knockdown. Pharmacological NNMT inhibition was evaluated in bleomycin-induced dermal fibrosis. RESULTS: NNMT was upregulated in SSc skin across independent cohorts and enriched in disease-expanded myofibroblast states. NNMT knockdown altered the SAM/S-adenosylhomocysteine ratio and histone methylation patterns, and attenuated transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ)-induced profibrotic programs associated with ECM production, collagen synthesis and tissue remodelling. Mechanistically, NNMT supported TGFβ-induced activation of an ATF4/SOX9/SRF transcriptional network that contributed to ECM gene expression and collagen secretion. Pharmacological NNMT inhibition recapitulated key effects of NNMT depletion, suppressed disease-associated SSc fibroblast programs, and attenuated experimental dermal fibrosis in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify a TGFβ-NNMT-ATF4/SOX9/SRF regulatory network linking metabolic regulation to DF activation. Targeting NNMT may represent a therapeutic strategy to attenuate fibrosis in SSc.

title: The impact of HFE genotypes and iron loading on joint disease: evidence for HFE-associated arthropathy without genetic haemochromatosis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aims to determine the association of recognised HFE genotypes with arthropathy fulfilling European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) haemochromatosis arthropathy (HA) classification criteria (CC), and the contributory role of iron loading. METHODS: We analysed 373 participants from the EULAR HA inception cohorts: group 1, C282Y homozygous with significant iron overload (n = 154); group 2A, C282Y homozygous without significant iron overload (n = 27); group 2B, other HFE genotypes irrespective of iron status (n = 72); group 3 (osteoarthritis/calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy controls without iron overload (n = 120). Group 2 were selected from rheumatology patients with persistent unexplained joint pain, potential HA, and/or pre-existing genotyping. Between-group comparisons and genotype-stratified analyses were performed. In group 2, associations among ferritin, transferrin saturation, and HA-CC fulfilment were assessed using regression analyses. RESULTS: HA-CC were fulfilled in 71.4% of group 1, 22.2% group 2A, 43.1% group 2B, and 6.7% group 3 (P < .001 all comparisons). Compared with group 3, group 2 demonstrated significantly higher prevalence of HA-CC fulfilment and 5 HA-CC features (P < .003 all items), including participants with H63D variants. Ferritin levels and transferrin saturation were not associated with HA-CC fulfilment odds ratio (OR) 1.000 per 1 µg/L increase, 95% CI: 1.000-1.001, P = .28; OR 0.98 per 1% increase, 95% CI: 0.96-1.01, P = .14, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: A substantial proportion of individuals without haemochromatosis but carrying HFE genotypes fulfil EULAR HA-CC, without an association with ferritin levels or transferrin saturation. This supports a potential iron-independent contribution of HFE variants to arthropathy. Although 'haemochromatosis arthropathy' is found in people with genetic haemochromatosis, 'HFE associated arthropathy without genetic haemochromatosis' describes metacarpophalangeal and/or ankle joint disease with any HFE genotype.

title: Global burden and economic cost of musculoskeletal disorders in the working-age population, 1990-2023
